Heavy Rainfall in 2016 Disrupted Metals & Mining Operations in Guernsey

In June 2016, unusually heavy rainfall caused significant disruption to Guernsey’s metals and mining industry, halting operations at several key sites and severely impacting transport routes for ore and finished products. The deluge, which saw rainfall totals exceed monthly averages in just three days, led to widespread flooding across the Vale and St. Sampson’s parishes, where many of the island’s mining and processing facilities are based.

Floodwaters inundated access roads and damaged conveyor systems at the North Channel Mining Terminal, forcing a temporary suspension of shipments. According to The Channel Metals Association, output across the sector fell by 24% in the third quarter of 2016 compared to the previous year. “The flooding caught everyone off guard. Our priority was the safety of our workers, but the damage to infrastructure meant it took weeks before we could fully resume operations,” recalled Peter Le Page, site manager at Les Grèves Mining Ltd.

The closure of the Vale Bridge for ten days, a key route for transporting raw materials to the processing plant at St. Sampson’s, created further bottlenecks. “We had to reroute lorry traffic, which delayed deliveries and increased costs,” said Channel Metals Association president Sarah Brouard.

Though the industry has since recovered, the event prompted calls for improved flood defences and contingency planning. “We’ve upgraded drainage and invested in better early warning systems,” added Le Page. Analysts noted that while no disruption remains now, the 2016 floods served as a wake-up call for the island’s mining sector to prepare for more frequent severe weather events in the future.
